findings.description: The check looks only at the last path component, never its parents. A dir under a parent another local user controls passes, and that user can swap it after the check, so the window loads their `settings.json` hooks.
findings.body:
**`namedConfigDir` checks only the last path component, so the attacker decision 106 names can still get past it.**

Decision 106 says the ownership check exists because "a dir another local user made first, under `/tmp` say, would run that user's commands in each." The check only `lstat`s and `stat`s `named` itself:

```ts
mkdirSync(named, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 });
...
const link = lstatSync(named, { throwIfNoEntry: false });
const dir = statSync(named, { throwIfNoEntry: false });
const uid = process.getuid?.();
if (!dir?.isDirectory() || link?.uid !== uid || dir.uid !== uid || (dir.mode & 0o022) !== 0) {
```

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/pupitre/blob/3f55c00a0e7829e544a410fae2256e548afa6c24/src/claude/session-runtime.service.ts#L345-L368

There is no `realpath`, no check on any parent, and no path normalization. Three inputs get through:

- **A parent another user owns.** Take `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=/tmp/w4b/claude`, where another user created `/tmp/w4b` first. pup creates `claude` inside it, mode 0700 and owned by the operator, so the check passes. Because that user owns the parent, they can rename `claude` away and put their own dir with a `settings.json` that names hooks in its place. They have time to do it while `preseedTrust`, `which`, the tmux spawn and Claude Code's startup run. The next launch refuses the swapped dir, but the window that already started keeps its hooks.
- **A link in the middle of the path.** With `/tmp/link -> /home/op/cfg` and `named=/tmp/link/claude`, `lstat` follows the middle link and sees the operator-owned target. The link's owner can repoint it later.
- **A trailing slash.** Tab completion gives `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=/tmp/w4b/`. With a trailing `/`, `lstat` follows a final symlink, so `link.uid` is the target's owner and not the link's. That defeats the line-357 guard ("one another user owns can be repointed after this check").

Windows run with bypass-permissions, so the planted hooks run as the operator. Decision 106's tests cover only a root-owned dir, a link to one, a writable dir and a file.

**Fix:**

1. Strip trailing slashes before the `lstat`.
2. Walk every component of the literal path and every parent of `realpathSync(named)`.
3. Require each one to be owned by the operator or root, and either not group- or other-writable or sticky (sticky `/tmp`, `/` and `/home` still pass).

findings.description: Duplicated Code. `readSessionEnv` hand-rolls the guarded read (`openSync(... O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`, `fstatSync`, `isFile()`, size cap, `closeSync` in `finally`) that `readPlainFile(path, { followLinks: false })` in `src/adapters/capability.utils.ts:21` already provides. The copy also loses the helper's capped read loop: `readFileSync(fd)` reads to EOF, so a session appending between the `fstat` and the read gets past the 4 KiB cap.

`transcriptDir`'s new `claudeDir` parameter has no production caller passing it (general.md §Altitude). `session-lifecycle.service.ts:659` and `dashboard.service.ts:199` still use the `~/.claude` default, so its JSDoc's "`claudeDir` is the window's (`claudeUserDir`)" holds for no real call. Thread the dir in or drop the param.

`sessionEnvAllowed()` is a one-caller wrapper that only formats the private list for the refusal at `src/cli/index.ts:904` (general.md §Altitude). Export `SESSION_ENV_ALLOWED`, or have `refusedSessionEnv` return the whole refusal text.

`pup audit --sweep` checks the config dir only inside `createOrRefuse`, after `auditProject` has run the full measurement. A relative or refused `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` therefore wastes a whole audit before the one-line refusal. Call `configDirOrRefuse(repoPath)` right after `refusedUnsandboxed()` when `opts.sweep` is set. This is also the only launch path the relative-dir test table doesn't cover.

`--session-env` is parsed with `parseGateEnv`, a gate-env-named helper, so a gate-specific change to it would silently change `--session-env` too. Rename it to something neutral such as `parseEnvNames`, which also removes the comment explaining the reuse.

The new `--session-env` tests sit between the decision-48 comment and the `lets the conductor run init` test it explains, so that comment now reads as describing the refusal tests. Move the new block above the comment or below that test.

The `vi.mock('../claude/session-runtime.service.js')` factory now repeats `await importOriginal<typeof import(...)>()` nine times, six of them new. Bind `const actual = await importOriginal<...>()` once and read each real export from it.

The CLI refusal test repeats 10 names that `session-runtime.test.ts` already covers over 32. It also hard-codes the full allowed-list sentence, so adding an allowed name means editing production code and both test files. One or two cases matched on the refusal prefix would test the wiring.

Decision 106's ~20-line *Tests.* paragraph restates test names and cases the test files already carry, and it will rot as cases change. Cut it to the non-obvious facts: the real-tmux run covers `;` and `\;` values, and `show-environment -g` stays free of `CLAUDE*`.

The closed-list-vs-denylist rationale is written out both in decision 106 and in the `SESSION_ENV_ALLOWED` JSDoc: the same namespaces, peer channel, credentials, loaders and `SETTABLE_VARS`. Cut the JSDoc to "closed list; see decision 106" plus the one-line WHY that a session can write the file.

`namedConfigDir`'s JSDoc says the dir is "made private when missing, so the trust seeded in it skips the dialog". Decision 106 gives the real reason: the 0700 mode lets the dir pup makes pass the same ownership and writability check. Reword the JSDoc to match.
